findings.text: This is the Athena site, but the title and almost the whole page are about another project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena first sees a heading about a tool they may never have heard of.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> / h1 "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: The opening lines do say clearly what Athena is and how it differs from similar tools: one model does the work, another checks it, and costs are recorded. This is the only description of Athena on the page, and nothing shows that request-to-change flow in action.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The page explains why the study is here: it shows what Athena can do. But Athena was just described as a tool that changes code, and the page never says whether studies are a main feature or a side capability. A newcomer can't tell which one they would actually use.
findings.source: "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project, taken at one fixed commit... Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it"

findings.text: A next step is easy to find: it is linked from the header and has concrete commands. But there is no clone command, no list of prerequisites (Rust toolchain, model API keys), and no description of what `athena ask` will output or change.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: Most of the page is a detailed state machine with exit codes 75 and 1, places-held, and pending-close records, plus 44 claims with line citations. That level of detail suits someone checking firstmate's internals, but it buries Athena's own message for a newcomer.
Every statement is linked to a claim, and every claim to source lines at the pinned commit. This shows Athena's main promise, traceability, in a way a reader can check. That part works well.
findings.source: "Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it; the claims, with links to their sources, are listed at the end."

findings.text: The "Start here" section and its short glossary give a quick way into firstmate. Even so, several terms are defined twice on the page (for example "in scope", "red", "yolo"), which adds length without adding meaning.
Athena's internal terms leak through to the reader: "job", "recorded boundary", and a `studies/` folder that is neither located nor linked. A newcomer can't follow these.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "The job gave no recorded boundary for running firstmate"; About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/"
